newsitem.title: ROMANIA: SOCCER-STEAUA EYES DIVORCE FROM ROMANIA MILITARY.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-STEAUA EYES DIVORCE FROM ROMANIA MILITARY.

text.p: Romania's top soccer club Steaua Bucharest is hoping to divorce its life-long partner of the past 50 years -- the ex-communist country's military establishment.

New club president Marcel Puscas wants to remove the current Romanian champions and cup holders from the umbrella of the army, which has ruled Steaua's destiny since the team was created in 1947 in the mould of Soviet-style sports rules.

But even after the defeat of ex-communists by centrists in last year's election, a new Defence Ministry clearly has other ideas and is no hurry to let go of the Balkan country's most illustrious team.
Steaua ('Star' in Romanian) swept to glory in 1986 when they beat Spain's Barcelona on penalties to win the European Cup.
Their international fortunes have been on the wane since the 1989 fall of Communism, but Steaua, Romanian champions for the past five years, still dominate the home scene.
Since he took over earlier this year, Puscas has tried to steer Steaua away from the army.

"Steaua must go free from communist-era subordination to the defence ministry, when the fate of soccer games was decided by Communist party leaders rather than on the field," Puscas said in an interview.

Former Steaua patrons include relatives of Romania's late hardline ruler Nicolae Ceausescu -- his brother Ilie, an army general and former deputy Defence Minister, and the dictator's elder son, Valentin.

Local sports media say Valentin Ceausescu played a major role in engineering Steaua's rise to their 1986 European Cup victory. Steaua qualified again for the European Cup final in 1989, but lost 4-0 against Italy's AC Milan.
Privileges came with a military uniform, but Steaua' soccer players also had to bow to army rigour.
Shortly before Ceausescu's overthrow and execution in a 1989 revolt, Steaua sweeper Miodrag Belodedici defected to former Yugoslavia to play for Belgrade's Red Star.
Belodedici, aged 25 at the time and an army captain, was tried in absentia by a Romanian military court and sentenced to 10 years in jail on treason charges.

The Defence Ministry in post-communist Romania has long since been turned over to a civilian chief, but the current office holder, Victor Babiuc, made plain last month he has no intention of relinquishing control over Steaua.
He appointed an army colonel, Cristian Gatu, to head the soccer team's parent body, Steaua sports club, with the title of "commander of the military club". Gatu replaced a general.
Club officials remain convinced that reforms bode well for Steaua's planned divorce from the military.

"We have taken the first steps to gain our independence from the Defence Ministry, which does not oppose our plans," said Puscas, for whom "independent status" means a chance of new glamour for his team.
Steaua must still clear difficult hurdles, such as the loss of subsidies from the army and the uncertainty of gaining powerful sponsors in exchange.

Puscas admits that Steaua's shaky finances work against change, despite big hard-currency earnings from the transfer of star players to Western clubs. "Steaua's financial sources appear to have dried up," he said.
The club's finances are under close scrutiny, with investigators examining what happened to some $15 million from post-1989 transfers abroad.
Not all club officials agree with the divorce, among them former trainer Dumitru Dumitriu, who resigned in protest last month.
"Steaua's successes derive from the club's old organisation. I don't see why it should be changed," said Dumitriu, who has signed to coach AEK Athens of Greece.
Steaua's arch-rivals Dinamo Bucharest are half-way through moves to scrap their Communist-era subordination to the Interior Ministry.
A third Bucharest team, Rapid, swapped their old patrons -- the Transport Ministry -- for a private sponsor in 1993.
Steaua's new coach, Mihai Stoichita, says he wants to use young blood -- the players' average age is 23 -- to restore the team's faded glory.
"Steaua will overcome the present difficulties and regain their dazzle, sticking to their tradition of high technical skills," Stoichita said. REUTER
